```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# Show stores below the temporary folder as `<tempdir>/...`, use UTC and a
# fixed width so that the output is the same on every machine.
local({
  dirs <- unique(c(
    normalizePath(tempdir(), winslash = "/", mustWork = FALSE),
    normalizePath(tempdir(), winslash = "\\", mustWork = FALSE),
    tempdir()
  ))
  hide <- function(x) {
    for (d in dirs) x <- gsub(d, "<tempdir>", x, fixed = TRUE)
    x
  }
  for (h in c("output", "message", "warning", "error")) {
    old <- knitr::knit_hooks$get(h)
    knitr::knit_hooks$set(stats::setNames(
      list(local({
        old <- old
        function(x, options) old(hide(x), options)
      })),
      h
    ))
  }
})
old_options <- options(width = 80, cli.width = 120, cli.hyperlink = FALSE)
old_tz <- Sys.getenv("TZ", unset = NA)
Sys.setenv(TZ = "UTC")
# Geocoding needs h3o, rasters need terra: chunks that use them run only
# when they are installed.
has_h3o <- requireNamespace("h3o", quietly = TRUE)
has_terra <- requireNamespace("terra", quietly = TRUE)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sf))
```

rcs stores `sf` objects and `terra` rasters next to tables, in the same
store and with the same functions. This vignette shows what the package
adds to geospatial data when it writes them, and how to read only the rows
that intersect an area. It assumes you have read `vignette("rcs")`.

Geocoding needs the package h3o, and rasters need terra. Both are
suggested, not required; the code below that uses them runs only when they
are installed.

```{r setup}
library(rcs)
library(sf)
st <- store_connect(file.path(tempdir(), "geo-store"), create = TRUE)
```

## Write an `sf` object

`rcs_sim_polygons()` returns simulated polygons in a box of open ocean,
between longitudes −30 and −24 and latitudes 6 and 9: small squares and
hexagons, a few large and long thin shapes, multipolygons and one empty
geometry. `rcs_sim_points()` and `rcs_sim_lines()` give points and lines in
the same box.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
polys <- rcs_sim_polygons(500, seed = 1)
polys
```

An `sf` object is written like a table. The dataset's kind becomes
`geospatial`, and its coordinate reference system (CRS) is kept in the
catalog. Any CRS can be used.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
store_write(st, polys, "shapes/polygons",
  title = "Polygons",
  description = "Simulated polygons in open ocean.",
  key = "id"
)
```

Two files were written: the data, and an *index table*, explained below.

## What the package adds, and why

A spatial filter on a large dataset should not read every geometry. To
let the Parquet reader skip rows without looking at geometries, the package
adds three columns when it writes an `sf` object:

- `h3`: an H3 cell. H3 divides the globe into hexagonal cells at 16
  resolutions; at resolution 5, the default, a cell covers about 250 km².
  `h3` is the cell that holds the largest part of the geometry, stored as a
  64-bit integer and read back as an H3 cell vector (class `rcs_h3`, see
  below).
- `bbox`: the bounding box of the geometry, four numbers (`xmin`, `ymin`,
  `xmax`, `ymax`).
- `.rcs_id`: a row number, unique within the dataset, used to link rows to
  the index table. Reads drop it unless it is asked for.

Rows are sorted by `h3` before they are written, so rows that lie close
together sit in the same file and the same blocks of rows. A filter on `h3`
and `bbox` is a comparison of plain numbers, which the Parquet reader
applies before it reads any geometry.

A geometry that crosses the edge of its cell also lies in other cells. The
*index table* `<dataset>__h3` lists every such row with every cell it
touches. It is written, replaced and deleted with its dataset, and is
hidden unless asked for:

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
print(st, index = TRUE)
```

`h3` and `bbox` come back with the data. `store_h3_hex()` turns the cell
columns of a data frame into the 15-character text form that other H3
tools use:

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
x <- store_read(st, "polygons", geometry = FALSE)
store_h3_hex(x)
```

## H3 cells in R

A cell column read from a store has class `rcs_h3`: a `bit64::integer64`
vector holding the same 64 bits that Parquet stores, filters and sorts,
printed as hex in the console, in tibbles and in `sf` objects.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
cells <- x$h3[1:3]
cells
class(cells)
```

Comparison, sorting, joins and `dplyr::bind_rows()` work as for
`integer64`, and joining an `rcs_h3` column with an `integer64` column
gives `rcs_h3`. Subsetting, `c()`, `rep()`, `unique()`, `sort()` and
`rev()` keep the class. `as.character()` gives decimal strings, exactly as
for `integer64` (the package relies on that for partition values and keys);
`rcs_h3_hex()` gives the hex strings of any cell vector: `rcs_h3`,
`integer64`, hex text in any case, h3o `H3` cells, or doubles.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
as.character(cells)
rcs_h3_hex(cells)
rcs_h3_hex(toupper(rcs_h3_hex(cells)))
```

A double cannot hold a cell exactly (cells are above 2^53), so a double
gives a warning, and a cell whose last bits were lost no longer validates:

```{r, eval = has_h3o, error = TRUE}
rcs_h3_hex(600496630537388031)
```

Inside a DuckDB connection prepared by the package, a SQL macro of the same
name gives the same strings, so `dplyr::mutate(cell = rcs_h3_hex(h3))`
runs lazily in DuckDB (see `vignette("duckdb")`). The Arrow engine cannot
translate it (`Expression not supported in Arrow`): there, call
`rcs_h3_hex()` after `collect()`.

Data that reach R by another route (`arrow::read_parquet()` on a stored
file, a DuckDB query of your own) carry only the storage types: plain
64-bit integers instead of cells, character instead of factor, and so on.
`store_restore_types()` gives back the R types recorded in the catalog,
cells included, without reading any file:

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
file <- list.files(file.path(tempdir(), "geo-store", "shapes", "polygons"),
  pattern = "\\.parquet$", full.names = TRUE
)[[1]]
raw_cols <- arrow::read_parquet(file, col_select = c("id", "h3"))
class(raw_cols$h3)
class(store_restore_types(raw_cols, st, "shapes/polygons")$h3)
```

## Read the rows in an area

`intersects` keeps the rows whose geometry intersects a query shape: an
`sf`, `sfc` or `bbox` object with a CRS.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
query <- st_sfc(
  st_polygon(list(rbind(
    c(-28.5, 6.5), c(-26, 6.5), c(-27.2, 8.5), c(-28.5, 6.5)
  ))),
  crs = 4326
)
inside <- store_read(st, "polygons", intersects = query)
nrow(inside)
```

The read works in steps. It keeps only the files whose extent overlaps the
query's box, reads the candidate rows (those whose `bbox` overlaps the
query's box), and finally tests the candidates exactly with
`sf::st_intersects()`, on the sphere or in the plane as described in
"Geocoding engines" below. When the query's box is much larger than the query
(a thin diagonal strip, a line), or the query crosses the antimeridian, the
H3 cells help: the read then also finds the cells the query touches, keeps
only files whose range of cells matches, and keeps only rows whose `h3`, or
a cell in the index table, is one of them. The result is the same as
filtering everything in memory:

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
setequal(inside$id, st_filter(polys, query)$id)
```

The query may be in another CRS than the data; it is transformed first.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
query_utm <- st_transform(query, 32626)
nrow(store_read(st, "polygons", intersects = query_utm))
```

### Candidates only: `exact = FALSE`

The exact test needs the geometries. With `exact = FALSE`, or with
`geometry = FALSE`, the read returns the candidate rows: every intersecting
row and some rows that only come close. A message says so.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
candidates <- store_read(st, "polygons",
  intersects = query, geometry = FALSE
)
nrow(candidates)
```

This is useful when the next step is a join on another column, or when an
approximate answer is enough and the geometries are large.

### H3 cells as query

The query can also be one or more H3 cells, of any resolution: as text,
as `bit64::integer64` or as an h3o `H3` vector. Each stands for its cell
polygon. A plain number is refused, because a double cannot hold an H3
cell exactly.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
cell <- store_h3_hex(x$h3[1])
cell
store_read(st, "polygons", intersects = cell, columns = c(id, cat))
```

A cell finer than the stored resolution works too; a message says that the
stored resolution is coarser.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
fine <- h3o::h3_from_xy(7.5, -27.5, 8L)
nrow(store_read(st, "polygons", intersects = fine))
```

### In a lazy query

`store_intersects()` adds the same filter to a lazy query from
`store_open()`, where it combines with the dplyr verbs:

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
store_open(st, "polygons") |>
  store_intersects(query) |>
  dplyr::filter(cat == "a") |>
  dplyr::select(id, area) |>
  dplyr::collect()
```

## One file per cell: `partition = "h3"`

`partition = "h3"` writes one file per H3 parent cell. The package picks the
finest resolution at which the number of files stays at most `max_files`
and names the partition column after it (`h3_p2` below: cells of
resolution 2). A spatial read then opens only the files of the cells near
the query. For large datasets this makes small spatial reads several times
faster, most of all from a cloud bucket (see the article "Benchmark: which
steps of the spatial filter pay off").

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
store_write(st, polys, "shapes/polygons_by_cell",
  title = "Polygons by cell",
  description = "Simulated polygons in open ocean, one file per H3 cell.",
  key = "id",
  partition = "h3",
  max_files = 10
)
```

The work counters show which files a read opened:

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
small <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(
  c(xmin = -29.5, ymin = 6.2, xmax = -29.2, ymax = 6.5),
  crs = st_crs(4326)
))
options(rcs.trace = TRUE)
near <- store_read(st, "polygons_by_cell", intersects = small)
trace <- rcs_trace()
options(rcs.trace = FALSE)
trace[trace$counter == "file_open", c("detail", "n")]
```

One data file of seven was opened. The query is a compact box, so the box
test alone selects the rows, and the index table is not read.

## Without H3: `geocode = FALSE`

`geocode = FALSE` writes the geometries with their `bbox` only: no `h3`
column and no index table, so writing skips the geocoding. A spatial read
then filters by bounding boxes alone: as fast for compact queries, slower
for queries much smaller than their box, and always complete.
`partition = "h3"` cannot be combined with it.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
store_write(st, polys, "shapes/polygons_boxes",
  title = "Polygons, boxes only",
  description = "Simulated polygons in open ocean, without H3 cells.",
  key = "id",
  geocode = FALSE
)
nrow(store_read(st, "polygons_boxes", intersects = query))
```

## Prepare data in memory

Three verbs do in memory, without a store, what a write adds and a read
returns:

- `rcs_geo_add()` adds `h3`, `bbox` and, with `parents`, one column
  `h3_p<r>` per coarser resolution `r` (the parent cell of `h3`, handy for
  grouping). The values equal those a write computes with the same `h3_res`
  and `geocode_engine`.
- `rcs_geo_index()` gives the rows of the index table: one line per row
  and cell it touches, with the share of the row's area (or length) in
  that cell, keyed by a column of yours instead of `.rcs_id`.
- `rcs_geo_strip()` removes the package's columns (`.rcs_id`, `h3`,
  `h3_main`, `bbox`, every `h3_p<r>`), so that data read with `collect()`
  go back to the form they were written from.

They keep the order of rows and columns; new columns go just before the
geometry column.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
prepared <- rcs_geo_add(polys, h3_res = 5, parents = 3)
prepared[1:3, ]
rcs_geo_index(polys, "id")
```

`store_write()` accepts prepared data. It drops `.rcs_id`, computes `h3`
and `bbox` itself, and compares them with the columns supplied: equal
values are accepted silently, so a raw and a prepared write of the same
data give the same version. The resolution is taken from the supplied
cells when `h3_res` is not given. The `h3_p<r>` columns are stored as user
columns, as cells; with `partition = "h3"`, a supplied column equal to the
partition column the write chooses serves as that column.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
store_write(st, prepared, "shapes/prepared",
  title = "Prepared polygons",
  description = "Simulated polygons in open ocean, prepared in memory.",
  key = "id"
)
```

Supplied values that differ (cells computed by another engine or
resolution, or edited by hand) stop the write, which names the rows and
the engine it used:

```{r, eval = has_h3o, error = TRUE}
tampered <- prepared
tampered$h3[3] <- tampered$h3[4]
store_write(st, tampered, "shapes/tampered",
  title = "Tampered polygons",
  description = "Simulated polygons with one cell changed.",
  key = "id"
)
```

The round trip gives the raw data back: the same attributes, the same
geometries (identical WKB) and the same CRS, once both are ordered by the
key.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
back <- store_open(st, "shapes/prepared") |>
  dplyr::collect() |>
  rcs_geo_strip()
back <- back[order(back$id), ]
names(back)
all.equal(
  tibble::as_tibble(st_drop_geometry(back)),
  tibble::as_tibble(st_drop_geometry(polys))
)
identical(st_as_binary(st_geometry(back)), st_as_binary(st_geometry(polys)))
st_crs(back) == st_crs(polys)
```

## Geocoding engines

A geometry can be valid in the plane and invalid on the sphere, where H3
cells live: a duplicated consecutive vertex, or a spike that almost
touches an edge. Two such polygons, added to the simulated ones:

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
wkt <- c(
  "POLYGON((-27.2 7.1, -26.9 7.1, -26.9 7.1, -26.9 7.4, -27.2 7.4, -27.2 7.1))",
  paste0(
    "POLYGON((-27.2 7.1, -26.9 7.1, -26.9 7.4, -27.05 7.4, ",
    "-27.05 7.1000000001, -27.06 7.4, -27.2 7.4, -27.2 7.1))"
  )
)
odd <- st_sf(
  id = 501:502, area = NA_real_, cat = "z",
  geometry = st_as_sfc(wkt, crs = 4326)
)
s2::s2_is_valid(odd)
mixed <- rbind(polys, odd)
```

`geocode_engine` says how the cells of rows that cross cell edges are
computed. Each such row is checked on the sphere on its own; rows inside
one cell get the same cell from every engine.

- `"auto"` (the default): valid rows are geocoded on the sphere. An
  invalid row is rebuilt by s2; when the rebuilt copy keeps its area
  (length for lines) within the option `rcs.s2_rebuild_tol` (default
  `1e-3`), its cells are used, otherwise the row is geocoded in the plane
  instead.
- `"s2"`: on the sphere; invalid rows are rebuilt by s2.
- `"planar"`: every crossing row in the plane, as `sf` sees it with
  `sf_use_s2(FALSE)`. Slower; for data drawn and checked in the plane.

Rebuilt copies serve only for the cells: the stored geometry is unchanged.
One warning names the keys of the rows that were rebuilt or geocoded in
the plane:

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
store_write(st, mixed, "shapes/mixed",
  title = "Polygons with invalid ones",
  description = "Simulated polygons, two of them invalid on the sphere.",
  key = "id"
)
store_describe(st, "shapes/mixed")$entry$geocode_engine
```

The engine is recorded with the dataset; an update uses it, and an update
that asks for another engine stops. Rows whose box spans 180 degrees or
more (around a pole, across the antimeridian) are always geocoded on the
sphere. For data in a projected CRS, the cells are computed the same way
on a copy in EPSG:4326. The same rows give the same cells and the same
version every time.

### The exact test on reads

`exact_engine` of `store_read()` and `store_intersects()` chooses where the
exact test runs. By default (`NULL`) it follows the dataset's engine:
`"s2"` on the sphere, `"planar"` in the plane, and `"auto"` on the sphere
for candidate rows valid there and in the plane for the others, so that an
invalid row never makes s2 fail. Datasets without a recorded engine
(written before engines were recorded, or with `geocode = FALSE`) follow
the session's `sf::sf_use_s2()`. `"s2"`, `"planar"` and `"session"`
override it. Data in a projected CRS are always tested in the
plane of their CRS.

```{r, eval = has_h3o}
near_odd <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(
  c(xmin = -27.1, ymin = 7.2, xmax = -27.0, ymax = 7.3),
  crs = st_crs(4326)
))
store_read(st, "shapes/mixed", intersects = near_odd, columns = id)$id
store_read(st, "shapes/mixed",
  intersects = near_odd, columns = id, exact_engine = "planar"
)$id
```

Both reads find the two invalid rows. With `exact_engine = "session"` and
`sf::sf_use_s2(TRUE)`, the exact test would run on the sphere for every row
and stop at them.

## Rasters

A `terra::SpatRaster` is written as one Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF, a format
that lets a reader fetch only the tiles it needs. `rcs_sim_raster()`
returns a simulated three-layer raster over the same box.

```{r, eval = has_terra}
grid <- rcs_sim_raster(seed = 1, nrow = 200, ncol = 200)
store_write(st, grid, "grids/simulated",
  title = "Simulated raster",
  description = "A simulated three-layer raster in open ocean."
)
```

`store_read()` opens the raster through GDAL. `intersects` crops it to the
query's bounding box, rounded outwards to whole cells.

```{r, eval = has_terra}
area <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(
  c(xmin = -28, ymin = 7, xmax = -27, ymax = 8),
  crs = st_crs(4326)
))
store_read(st, "grids/simulated", intersects = area)
```

A raster has one file: it cannot be partitioned or updated, only replaced.
Filters, `columns`, `geometry` and `exact` do not apply to rasters, and
`store_open()` and `store_sample()` refuse them.

## Shapes across the antimeridian or around a pole

Geometries that cross the antimeridian (longitude ±180°) or contain a pole
are stored and found correctly. The package detects them, finds their cells
on the sphere, and always lists them in the index table, because their
bounding box, which may span all longitudes, says little about where they
lie. Query shapes of this kind are handled the same way. These rows are
defined on the sphere and are geocoded there by every engine: a read whose
exact test runs in the plane (`exact_engine = "planar"`, or the session
rule with `sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)`) is not guaranteed to find them.
`rcs_sim_polygons(special = TRUE)` adds one such polygon of each kind,
for trying this out.

```{r, include = FALSE}
unlink(file.path(tempdir(), "geo-store"), recursive = TRUE)
options(old_options)
if (is.na(old_tz)) Sys.unsetenv("TZ") else Sys.setenv(TZ = old_tz)
```
